children.name: Local and Air-Gapped Model Deployment
children.blurb: Local and air-gapped model deployment covers running a language model on hardware a legal team controls, either on a private network or on a machine with no outside connection at all.

children.name: Secure Storage and Networking for Legal Data
children.blurb: Secure storage and networking for legal data covers the systems that hold client files, matter records, privileged communications and court filings, and the connections that move that material between offices, courts, vendors and clients.

children.name: Timekeeping and Billing Narratives
children.blurb: Timekeeping and billing narratives covers the systems and practices that turn recorded work into the descriptions clients pay for, from the timer a lawyer starts before a call to the invoice line that reaches the client.

children.name: Firm Knowledge Management
children.blurb: Firm knowledge management covers how a law firm captures, stores, and retrieves what its lawyers know: precedent documents, matter files, research memos, clause banks, and the informal expertise held by individual attorneys.

children.name: Client Intake and Triage
children.blurb: Client intake and triage is the front end of legal service delivery, where a firm or legal department captures a new matter, checks for conflicts, and decides how it will be handled.

sections.body: Legal operations, infrastructure and security is the part of legal AI work that sits behind the visible drafting and research tools. It covers where models run, how confidential material is stored and moved, how time is captured and billed, how a firm's own knowledge is organised, and how new clients arrive and get sorted. In practice this is where artificial intelligence stops being a demo and becomes something a firm can run every day. Local and air-gapped deployment puts a model on hardware the firm controls, so client material never leaves the building. Secure storage and networking work keeps that material encrypted and segmented while still letting the right people reach it. Billing and intake tools apply language models to the routine text that surrounds legal work, which is often where the hours and the risk actually sit.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some of this is genuinely settled. Running an open-weight model on a firm's own server is now a normal engineering task, and the tooling for containers, private networking and encrypted storage is mature. Timekeeping narratives and client intake summaries are among the more reliable uses of language models because the output is short, checkable and easy for a person to correct. What is not solved is the harder middle. Retrieval over a firm's own documents still fails in quiet ways, permissions are hard to enforce consistently across systems, and a local model is only as private as the weakest machine that touches its data. Cost, latency and maintenance are real, and a small firm may not have the staff to run any of it well. Nothing here removes the need for human review, and none of it is a substitute for a firm's own security and compliance obligations.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages run from the ground up. Local and Air-Gapped Model Deployment is the foundation, covering where a model physically runs and what that means for confidentiality. Secure Storage and Networking for Legal Data takes the next layer, the encryption, access control and network design that keep that deployment safe. Timekeeping and Billing Narratives turns to the output side, using models to draft the descriptions that support a bill. Firm Knowledge Management deals with the firm's accumulated work product, how it is captured, indexed and retrieved. Client Intake and Triage sits at the front door, where new matters are described, sorted and routed. A reader new to the area should start with deployment and storage, then move to the three operational pages for the day to day uses.
